power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer related mortality, yet the role of lower airway microbiota in disease development and progression is incompletely defined.

We characterised the lung microbiome in an Australian cohort (lung cancer n=106, healthy n=10) using shotgun metagenomics and semi quantitative culture to evaluate microbial ecology across the tumour microenvironment (TME), contralateral airways, and oral cavity, to evaluate microbiome differences across early and late stage disease, and to quantify clinical covariate impacts on airway microbiota.
Diversity analyses, multivariable linear modelling, and culture based comparisons were performed, with adjustment for smoking pack years, sex, and tumour characteristics.

Results: Cumulative smoking exposure caused significant, progressive Neisseria subflava, Gemella sanguinis, and Rothia mucilaginosa depletion, alongside Streptococcus mitis enrichment, with Mogibacterium diversum uniquely depleted within the TME of smokers. β diversity in both early-and latestage bronchial washes (BWs) significantly diverged from healthy controls, whilst α diversity was significantly reduced in early-stage vs. late-stage BWs.
The early stage TME demonstrated significantly reduced microbial cultivability compared with healthy and other lung cancer BWs.

A small number of taxa were uniquely enriched (Sporothrix and Pseudomonas species) or depleted (Streptococcus parasanguinis, Streptococcus cristatus, R. mucilaginosa) within the TME, and 13 taxa were significantly enriched or depleted in both TME and contralateral airways compared with healthy airways.
Only adenocarcinoma showed distinct oral β diversity restructuring.
The lung cancer microbiome is characterised by early and progressive lower airway dysbiosis that is strongly shaped by tumour presence.
Our findings point to potential new avenues for microbiome based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer related mortality globally, and 1.8 million people are diagnosed every year 1 .
text.formatted: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer related mortality globally, and 1.8 million people are diagnosed every year <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: Despite recent treatment advances, lung cancer remains an insidious disease with poor prognosis, with five-year survival rates of 27% (68% for Stage I and 3% for Stage IV disease) 2,3

Given its largely asymptomatic nature until late-stage disease, coupled with its high mortality rate and significant socioeconomic burden, earlier diagnosis, improved therapeutic interventions, and prevention are essential for improving outcomes.
There is increasing recognition of the role microbes play in oncogenesis, with current estimates suggesting single-pathogen infections are linked to 12-16% of all human cancers 4, 5 .
text.formatted: There is increasing recognition of the role microbes play in oncogenesis, with current estimates suggesting single-pathogen infections are linked to 12-16% of all human cancers <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: However, major gaps remain in understanding the impact of microbial community changes (particularly microbiome dysbiosis) in lung cancer development, treatment response, and progression.

Most lung cancer microbiome studies have used 16S rRNA variable-region amplicon sequencing (metataxonomics) to profile lung tissue and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF), and to a lesser extent, sputum 6   .

Whilst these studies have reported the extratumoural or intratumoural enrichment of taxa such as Veillonella, Streptococcus, and Acidovorax [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] , enormous variability in study design, participant inclusion/exclusion criteria, specimen type/s, geographic region, and disease stage has made establishment of a consensus link challenging.

text.text: A recent meta-analysis of intratumoural 16S metataxonomic studies attempted to overcome this variability, identifying broad shifts such as increased Actinobacteria and Corynebacterium in tumour tissues 12.
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis of intratumoural 16S metataxonomic studies attempted to overcome this variability, identifying broad shifts such as increased Actinobacteria and Corynebacterium in tumour tissues <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, 16S rRNA metataxonomics remains inherently limited by poor species-level resolution, the exclusion of viruses and fungi, and high susceptibility to contaminant amplification in low-biomass environments.
Recent investigations have shifted towards shotgun metagenomics to more comprehensively profile lung cancer microbiota in tumour tissue 13, 14 or BALF [15] [16] [17] [18] [19] .

text.text: However, like 16S sequencing, metagenomic profiling has revealed a high degree of inter-study variability, with inconsistent alpha (α) and beta (β) diversity findings.
Furthermore, no single microbe has been found to be enriched or depleted in lung cancer airways (tumour tissues or BALF specimens) compared with control cohorts.

Like 16S-based studies, the lack of consensus is unsurprising due to differences in control groups (healthy individuals, people with benign lung diseases, normal adjacent lung tissues), statistical methodologies, clinical covariates, specimen collection and processing workflows, bioinformatic approaches, handling of background contamination, and environmental/geographical factors, along with small sample sizes.
To address some of these challenges, large-scale multicentre analyses have attempted to map tumourspecific microbiomes across various cancers, including lung cancer 20, 21 .

text.text: One such study, by Nejman and colleagues, undertook 16S-based analysis of 1526 tumours across seven cancer types.

Their analysis identified a significant enrichment of tobacco-degradation pathways in the lung tumours of smokers; however, due to the diverse and heterogeneous group of bacteria sharing these smoke-degrading metabolic capabilities, a uniform species-level signature was absent 20   .

Concurrently, the recent retraction of a large, retrospective cancer microbiome study due to bioinformatic artefacts 22 underscores the challenges of low-biomass sequencing and highlights the critical need for rigorous negative controls to account for kitome, bronchoscope, and upper respiratory tract contamination.

text.text: Although prior findings highlight the clinical potential of lung cancer microbiomics, significant knowledge gaps remain.

Specifically, the field has struggled to untangle the confounding effects of cumulative tobacco exposure from tumour-driven dysbiosis, often failing to isolate a true disease signature from the background smoking microbiome.

Furthermore, longitudinal mapping across early-and late-stage disease, particularly distinguishing localised changes within the tumour microenvironment (TME) from broader, systemic airway shifts, remains poorly defined.
Reliance on sequencing alone without functional or culture-based validation has also obscured true biomass and viability fluctuations.

Finally, no comprehensive shotgun metagenomic studies have been performed in Oceania lung cancer cohorts, hampering international generalisability due to unexplored geographical and cohort-specific variations.

To address these knowledge gaps, we employed shotgun metagenomics alongside semi-quantitative conventional culture to comprehensively characterise the extratumoural lung cancer microbiome in a prospective, single-centre cohort in Queensland (QLD), Australia.

This study delivers several key advances to the lung cancer microbiome field by combining anatomical site-specific metagenomic profiling, stage-stratified ecological modelling, and conventional culture validation.

Our most striking and novel finding is the identification of a distinct functional window in earlystage disease: early-stage TME BWs exhibited significantly reduced microbial cultivability compared to all other airway sites, pointing to a profound, transient suppression of commensal growth during early tumourigenesis.

Second, by leveraging a anatomically paired design across early-and late-stage cohorts, we demonstrate that lung cancer induces a progressive, systemic ecological destabilisation across the lower airways.

Third, our multivariable models successfully untangle complex environmental confounders, revealing that cumulative smoking drives broad commensal depletion (e.g., N. subflava, G. sanguinis, R. mucilaginosa), and M. diversum depletion is uniquely governed by a synergy between heavy smoking and localised tumour presence.

Beyond these novel biological insights, our workflow incorporates rigorous negative controls and multimodal culture-independent and culture-dependent validation, providing a robust framework for future biomarker discovery.

Nonetheless, a consistent pattern is evident across studies: that is, that lung cancer drives the depletion of protective commensals alongside the selective enrichment of opportunistically pathogenic taxa.
Collectively, our findings consolidate prior work showing that the TME fosters a distinct microbial niche that is independent of oral cavity topology and the contralateral lung.
Culture-independent sequencing approaches cannot readily detect absolute microbial load differences due to their inherent compositional data format.

As these technologies measure relative proportions rather than absolute numbers, a massive physical bloom of one taxon mathematically forces the apparent decline of others, masking true biomass fluctuations.
Integrating conventional culture into cultureindependent investigations therefore provides valuable orthogonal validation by quantifying cultivable microbial load across specimen types.
Furthermore, conventional culture distinguishes organisms that are metabolically active and capable of shaping the TME from those merely detectable as remnant DNA.
Despite these advantages, just one prior study has integrated culture-dependent and -independent techniques.

Culturing viable microbes directly from lung cancer specimens is critically important for understanding how specific organisms and strains actively contribute to local inflammation, modulate tumour associated immune responses, or influence tumour proliferation pathways.

Although our study did not undertake culturomics, our semi-quantitative agar scoring approach crucially identified significantly lower cultivable microbial growth in the early-stage TME compared with all other BW types (Figure 6).

text.text: This striking finding points to a critical period in early lung tumourigenesis, during which the TME transiently, yet profoundly, suppresses commensal microbial growth.

This localised suppression may reflect a hyperactive mucosal immune response: during early tumour development, the TME is characterised by an influx of macrophages and neutrophils, and the production of reactive oxygen species, thus creating a hostile zone for commensal microbes 52 .

text.text: Another possibility is the targeted secretion of antimicrobial peptides by the developing tumour, such as human β-defensins (e.g. hBD-1) 53.

text.text: Our observation offers unique opportunities for early-stage biomarker discovery and the development of new therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring a more favourable TME microbiome profile at a potentially critical juncture in lung cancer pathogenesis, and deserves further exploration.

Current literature is split on whether different histological subtypes are associated with microbiome alterations, although most studies have reported no significant α or β diversity differences [9] [10] [11] 17, 39, 42, 48, [54] [55] [56].

text.text: Although most prior lung cancer microbiome studies have not undertaken subtype specific comparisons, our findings diverge from those of Greathouse and colleagues, who reported Acidovorax, Klebsiella, Rhodoferax, and Anaerococcus enrichment in LUSC relative to LUAD tissue 11 ; however, a key distinction is that Greathouse and colleagues analysed tumour tissue.

text.text: Nevertheless, these contrasting observations underscore the need for future studies that directly interrogate tumour specific microbial signatures across histological and molecular subtypes, particularly in the context of increased genomic subclassification and precision based oncology 57 .

text.text: Our findings suggest that the extratumoural lung microbiome is not shaped by tumour histology; however, larger sample sizes, particularly for SCLC and rarer histological subtypes, would be needed for definitive confirmation.

Furthermore, unlike studies examining intratumoural tissue specimens, our analysis focused on extratumoural BWs, which may capture a broader airway community less acutely bound to local histological niches.

Although not explored in this study, functional profiling of lung cancer subtypes using host-microbe epigenomics, proteomics, or metabolomics may uncover biomarkers that are strongly linked to subtype.

Oral microbial signatures have been proposed as an appealing, non invasive biospecimen for lung cancer biomarker development, with several studies reporting taxonomic and oral microbiome compositional differences in lung cancer cohorts 39, 48, 49, 58, 59 .
text.formatted: Oral microbial signatures have been proposed as an appealing, non invasive biospecimen for lung cancer biomarker development, with several studies reporting taxonomic and oral microbiome compositional differences in lung cancer cohorts <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">59</ref> .

text.text: In our cohort, global comparisons revealed significant overarching structural divergence in the oral microbiome across lung cancer subtypes (PERMANOVA p=0.031; Figure S5A), accompanied by significant ecological destabilisation (betadispersion p=0.046), indicating that lung cancer presence disrupts the oral microbiome compared with the healthy baseline.
text.formatted: In our cohort, global comparisons revealed significant overarching structural divergence in the oral microbiome across lung cancer subtypes (PERMANOVA p=0.031; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">S5A</ref>), accompanied by significant ecological destabilisation (betadispersion p=0.046), indicating that lung cancer presence disrupts the oral microbiome compared with the healthy baseline.

text.text: Upon pairwise testing, it became clear that this global divergence was primarily driven by the LUAD cohort, as we observed significant β diversity differences between LUAD and healthy oral microbiota (FDR p=0.020), with a borderline difference between LUAD and LUSC (FDR p=0.050).

Despite this significant β diversity shift, we found no strong evidence that tumour-associated microbial patterns originate from oral cavity dysbiosis, and, reflective of the broad ecological destabilisation seen in LUAD, no taxa were consistently enriched or depleted in any subtype.

Instead, our findings support the hypothesis that distinct lung cancer-associated microbial signatures arise from local ecological selection pressures within the lower airways, aligning with prior work demonstrating clear divergence between TME and oral microbiota 48, 59 .
text.formatted: Instead, our findings support the hypothesis that distinct lung cancer-associated microbial signatures arise from local ecological selection pressures within the lower airways, aligning with prior work demonstrating clear divergence between TME and oral microbiota <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">59</ref> .

text.text: Taken together, our results indicate that further investigation of oral β diversity disturbances in LUAD cohorts is warranted; however, they temper enthusiasm for the use of oral sampling as a non-invasive lung cancer biomarker for other histological subtypes.

Our finding of unique P. trivialis enrichment in TME BWs (Figure 5) prompted us to further investigate this fluorescent, grass-dwelling bacterium 60 in our metagenomic reads using comparative genomics.

text.text: Despite this significant signal, none of our metagenomes possessed P. trivialis according to phylogenomic reconstruction; instead, a wide array of PFG taxa, including potentially novel species, were identified (Figure S6).

text.text: Whilst an incorrect taxonomic assignment by Kraken2, our P. trivialis finding nevertheless suggests that PFG bacteria may play an outsized role in the TME microbiome.

PFG species are rarely associated with human infections, typically affecting only immunocompromised people, but are common in soil and water, and can colonise human airways, skin, and the gastrointestinal tract.
Given that cancer patients receiving treatment frequently become immunocompromised, PFG infection may represent an unrecognised risk for this cohort.
As many PFG species likely cannot grow on MacConkey agar, we overlooked these taxa in our conventional culture-based assessments.

Future work will involve isolation and whole-genome sequencing of these organisms from lung cancer specimens, which in turn, will facilitate improvements in Kraken2 and other taxonomy-based bioinformatic tools.

Strengths of our study include its prospective design and our near-universal collection of paired tumour and contralateral BWs, alongside matched oral washes (n=92; 86.8% of participants), which permitted precise mixed-effects modelling that inherently controlled for intra-patient variability and topographical contamination.
However, we acknowledge several limitations.

Our lung cancer cohort possessed a substantially higher mean smoking history (31.8±16.5 pack-years) compared with healthy controls (3.3±2.3 pack-years), reflecting the inherent clinical difficulty in recruiting heavy-smoking healthy volunteers without underlying respiratory disease.
Although statistically adjusted, fully decoupling the smoking and lung cancer microbiomes requires longitudinally tracking heavy smokers who do not develop lung cancer.

Reliance on short-read sequencing limited taxonomic resolution, and bioinformatic decontamination was required to remove microbial DNA introduced by reagent and kit components, which potentially included real signal in our BWs.
Future low-biomass studies should prioritise certified DNA-free reagents to optimise signal-to-noise ratios and should integrate long-read sequencing to enhance species-level assignments.

Sampling was restricted to the extratumoural space; incorporating matched endobronchial/transbronchial biopsies or surgical resections is needed to confirm whether these signatures persist within the intratumoural niche.
We did not undertake selective culture and wholegenome sequencing of key taxa (e.g.
PFG species, N. subflava, M. diversum, P. thailandica, Sporothrix spp.) to confirm their presence in our clinical specimens.
The absence of matched blood and stool specimens precluded the evaluation of less invasive circulatory or faecal biomarkers.

Microbial anatomical gradient between the healthy oral cavity and lower airways in lung cancer and healthy participants.

Multivariable mixed-effects modelling (MaAsLin3), controlling for smoking pack-years and biological sex, demonstrated significant enrichment (dark orange) and depletion (dark blue) of microbial taxa within the tumour microenvironment (TME) and the contralateral airway relative to the participant's matched oral cavity baseline.

Both distal lung cancer sites shared strong microbiota commonalities (Pearson's r correlation: 0.986), characterised by the depletion of five core oral commensals (Streptococcus sanguinis, S. gordonii, S. oralis, Veillonella parvula, Actinomyces naeslundii), and enrichment of eight taxa, including five fungal species.

The inclusion of a healthy cohort baseline (left) confirms these ecological shifts are disease-specific phenomena rather than universal pan-airway gradients.
